topicName: Nature and nurture in brain development

cards.front: Why can two children raised in the same home still have brains that work differently?
cards.back: Because both **genes** and **environment** shape brain development. Inherited DNA gives one part of the difference, and each child's own experiences give another.
cards.hint: Think about what each child inherits and what each child experiences.

cards.front: How can experience change the wiring of the brain?
cards.back: Connections between neurones, called **synapses**, form, strengthen and are lost with use, so experience can reshape them.
cards.hint: Think about what happens to connections between cells over time.

cards.front: Why do researchers compare monozygotic and dizygotic twins?
cards.back: **Monozygotic** twins share virtually all their genes and dizygotic twins share about half, so if monozygotic pairs resemble each other more, genes probably contribute.

cards.front: What is an environmental influence on brain development?
cards.back: An effect on development that comes from factors outside the inherited genes, such as **nutrition**, learning or stress.
cards.hint: Think of the nurture side of the debate.

cards.front: What is a genetic influence on brain development?
cards.back: An effect on development that comes from the **genes** a person inherits. This is the nature side.

cards.front: Why does Huntington's disease show a genetic influence on the brain?
cards.back: It is caused by a **faulty version of a single gene** that is inherited, so neurones in parts of the brain stop working properly whatever the person's lifestyle.

cards.front: What did young animals reared in enriched cages show compared with those in bare cages?
cards.back: They developed a **thicker cortex** and more synapses than animals in bare cages.
cards.hint: Think about what the enriched cages provided.

cards.front: Calculate the monozygotic concordance when both twins show a feature in 24 of 30 pairs where at least one twin is affected.
cards.back: $\frac{24}{30}\times 100 = 80\%$. Divide pairs with both twins affected by pairs with at least one affected, then multiply by 100.
cards.hint: Concordance only counts pairs where at least one twin shows the feature.

cards.front: What is concordance in a twin study?
cards.back: The **percentage** of twin pairs in which both twins show a feature, counting only pairs where at least one twin shows it.

cards.front: Why is it wrong to think a monozygotic concordance below 100% means genes have no effect?
cards.back: Genes can still matter. A value below 100% shows that the **environment** also contributes to the feature.

cards.front: Why might identical twins look more alike than their genes alone explain?
cards.back: They may be treated more **alike** by other people, which can exaggerate how similar they are because of genes.
cards.hint: Think about how other people respond to each type of twin.

cards.front: How does phenylketonuria show that genes and environment can interact?
cards.back: The gene is unchanged, but a build-up of a substance from food damages the developing brain. A **carefully controlled diet** from early life prevents most of this damage.
cards.hint: Think about what changes the outcome when the gene itself stays the same.

cards.front: Name one environmental factor in early life that can limit brain growth.
cards.back: **Poor nutrition** in early life can limit brain growth.
